title: How to translate web page chrome mac: address bar, right-click and Settings
metaTitle: Translate a Web Page in Chrome on Mac: Steps and Settings
description: Translate a web page in Chrome on Mac from the address bar or right-click menu. Steps, Settings, and fixes for when the icon goes missing.
intro: To translate a web page in Chrome on Mac, click the Translate icon at the right end of the address bar and pick your language. You can also right-click an empty part of the page, choose Translate to, and select the language you want.
tldr: Click the Translate icon at the right end of the Chrome address bar, then pick your language.
Or right-click an empty part of the page and choose Translate to, followed by the language.
To translate only highlighted text, right-click the selection and choose Translate selection to.
Change default languages in More > Settings > Languages. Press ⌘ , to open Settings.
If translation fails, refresh the page first, then check the Google Translate settings.

blocks.text: Translate the whole page from the address bar

Open the page in Chrome first, and wait until the text has loaded. Look at the right end of the address bar, the long field at the top of the window that shows the web address. Google's help article says the Translate icon sits on the right side of that bar. Click it, pick the language you want, and Chrome translates the page text in place.

Chrome does not show the icon on every page. It appears when a page is in a language different from the one you use, so a page in your own language usually will not offer it. If you don't see the icon, you can still use the right-click menu on the same page. The next section shows how.
Use the right-click menu on the page

Right-click on an empty part of the page, away from links, images, and text fields. A menu opens with an item that reads Translate to, followed by a language name. Google's help article calls this Translate to [Language], so the exact words change with the language you pick. Select it, and the page translates.
On a Mac, you can also Control-click, or use a two-finger click on a trackpad. Both open the same context menu, so the Translate to item appears either way. Use whichever gesture feels faster to you.

items: Address bar: click the Translate icon on the right, then pick a language.
Whole page, right-click: choose Translate to, then the language name.
Selected text: highlight the words, right-click, and choose Translate selection to.
Different language: select More, then Choose another language.

blocks.text: Translate only the text you select

Sometimes you need one paragraph, not the whole page. Highlight the words you care about, right-click the selection, and choose Translate selection to, followed by your language. Only that selection changes. This is handy for one comment in a forum thread, a single caption in a photo gallery, or one line on a restaurant menu page. Use the whole page option when you need to read a full article.
A worked example: a Spanish recipe page

Say you find a recipe on a Spanish cooking site, and you read English but not Spanish. Open the page, wait for the ingredient list to load, and click the Translate icon at the right end of the address bar. Choose English. The ingredients and steps switch to English.

Measurements are the trickiest part of any translated recipe. If an amount looks odd, check it against the original page before you start cooking. Machine translation can misread units, so the extra check takes less time than a ruined dish.

Now say a friend reads German and wants the same page. Select More, then Choose another language, and pick German. The page translates again into German. You can switch the target language as many times as you need.

blocks.title: Older name for the icon
blocks.text: A 2020 Macworld guide tells you to click the Google Translate icon in the address bar. Google's current help article just says Translate icon. Both describe the same control at the right end of the address bar.
Set Chrome to translate languages on its own

Settings control what Chrome does without asking. Open More, then Settings, then Languages. You can also press ⌘ , to open Settings directly. The Languages page has a Google Translate section, and that section holds the translation controls covered in this guide.

blocks.text: Think about the two language lists. The automatic list means pages in those languages translate on their own. The never list means Chrome stops offering to translate those languages. If you ever told Chrome never to offer translation for a language, that language will never show the icon. Remove it from the never list to bring the icon back.
Translate a page outside Chrome with Google Translate

Sometimes the page is open in another browser, or you need a copy you can share. Go to translate.google.com and choose Websites. Paste the page address, and Google Translate opens a translated version. Google's help article mentions this option for pages outside Chrome, so use it when the Chrome steps don't fit your situation.
Why the translation fails or looks wrong

Start with the simplest fix. Google's help article says to refresh the page if Translate doesn't work. Click the reload button to the left of the address bar, then try the Translate icon again. Some pages load their text after the first screen appears, so the first attempt can miss part of the page.

items: Turn on Use Google Translate under Settings, Languages.
Check the never list for the page language and remove it if it is there.
Update Chrome through More, Help, About Google Chrome.
Try the right-click menu if the icon is missing.
Use translate.google.com with Websites if Chrome still refuses.

blocks.text: Translation quality varies. Chrome gives you a machine translation, so names, prices, dates, and legal terms need a second check. Read the original text for anything that involves money, a contract, or a medical decision. Machine translation is a reading aid, not a sign-off.
Keep Chrome updated so the menus match this guide

Chrome updates often, and menus shift between versions. To check yours, select More, then Help, then About Google Chrome. The page shows your version. If an update is ready, select Relaunch to apply it. Select Not now to wait until your next restart.

The help article has no Mac screenshots and no version number, so the steps here follow its wording. Google's Enterprise release notes list Chrome 152 as the newest stable release they show, dated September 1, 2026. Google's download page still says a new update arrives every four weeks. 9to5Google reports a two-week cycle starting with Chrome 153 on September 8, 2026.
Common mistakes people make

items: Looking for a keyboard shortcut to translate the page. Google's shortcut list has none for page translation, so use the icon or the right-click menu.
Changing the target language in Settings when you only wanted one page. Settings affects how Chrome translates pages, so use the icon for a one-time change.
Expecting a selection translation to change the whole page. It only changes the highlighted text.
Trusting the output for legal, medical, or financial text without checking the original.

blocks.text: Watch for the never list too. If the icon goes missing for one language, check Settings before you blame the page. The fix is almost always a setting, not the site.

Once the page reads the way you need, go back to your task. If you use Chrome for hours each day, the same few steps come back often. Lazur can point at the Translate icon or the Settings path while you learn them. See [Lazur in Chrome](/apps/chrome) for how it works on a web page.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to translate a web page in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Google's Chrome keyboard shortcut list does not include one for translating a page. Use the Translate icon at the right end of the address bar, or right-click the page. The shortcut list does include ⌘ , for Settings, which is the fastest way to reach the Languages page.

faq.question: Why is there no Translate icon in my address bar?
faq.answer: Chrome usually offers translation when a page is in a language other than the one you use, so pages in your own language won't show it. A language on your never list stays hidden too. Refresh the page, check Settings, Languages, and update Chrome if the menu still doesn't appear.

faq.question: Can I translate a page into English in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Choose English from the language list in the Translate icon menu, or right-click the page and choose Translate to English. To make English your default, set Translate into this language to English under More, Settings, Languages.

faq.question: What is the difference between translating a page and translating selected text?
faq.answer: Translating a page changes all the text on the page, through the address bar icon or the page right-click menu. Translating selected text changes only the words you highlight, through the right-click item Translate selection to. Use the selection option for a single sentence or quote.

faq.question: Can I translate a page that is open in Safari?
faq.answer: This guide covers Chrome only. Safari has its own controls, which this guide does not cover. You can copy the page address into translate.google.com, choose Websites, and read the translated copy there.

faq.question: Which Chrome version do these steps match?
faq.answer: Google's help article does not name a version and has no Mac screenshots, so these steps follow its wording. Google's Enterprise release notes list Chrome 152 as the newest stable release they show. Check More, Help, About Google Chrome to see your version.

faq.question: Is Chrome's translation accurate enough for contracts or medical pages?
faq.answer: Use it to understand a page, not to sign or act on it. Machine translation can misread context, names, and figures. Check the original text for anything involving money, a legal agreement, or a medical decision, and ask a qualified translator when it matters.

task: Translate a web page in Chrome on Mac
requirements: A Mac with Google Chrome installed
A web page open in a language you do not read
An internet connection, because translation runs through Google

steps.name: Open the page in Chrome
steps.text: Load the page in Google Chrome and wait until the text appears on screen. Pick a page in a language you do not read, because Chrome offers translation for pages in other languages. Let the page finish loading before you translate it.
steps.tip: Let the page finish loading, so the whole text goes into the translation.

steps.name: Find the Translate icon
steps.text: Look at the right end of the address bar, the long field at the top of the window. Google's help article says the Translate icon sits on the right side of that bar. Click it.
steps.tip: ⌘ L moves the cursor to the address bar. It does not open translation.

steps.name: Pick your language
steps.text: A list of languages opens. Select the language you want the page in. Chrome then translates the page text into that language.
steps.tip: If your language is not in the first list, use the More menu in step 6.

steps.name: Or use the right-click menu
steps.text: Right-click an empty part of the page, away from links, images, and text boxes. Choose Translate to, followed by the language name. Google's help article calls this Translate to [Language].
steps.tip: A two-finger click on a trackpad or Control-click does the same thing.

steps.name: Translate only selected text
steps.text: Highlight the words you want to translate. Right-click the highlighted words and choose Translate selection to, followed by your language. Only the selection changes.
steps.tip: Use this for one sentence or comment instead of a whole article.

steps.name: Change the target language
steps.text: Select More, then Choose another language if the language you need is not in the first list. Pick the target language. This sets the language Chrome translates into.
steps.tip: The More button is the three-dot menu at the top right of the Chrome window.

steps.name: Open Chrome Settings
steps.text: Press ⌘ , to open Settings, or select More, then Settings from the menu. Settings holds every translation control in this guide.
steps.tip: If you need to type a web address, ⌘ L jumps to the address bar.

steps.name: Open the Languages section
steps.text: In Settings, select Languages. Scroll to the Google Translate section. Here you can turn Use Google Translate on or off, and choose Translate into this language.
steps.tip: The Google Translate section is where the page translation controls live.

steps.name: Set the translate and never lists
steps.text: Under Automatically translate these languages, select Add languages to add one. Under Never offer to translate these languages, use Remove to take one off the list. Check both lists when a language behaves oddly.
steps.tip: Check the never list first if the icon is missing for one language.

steps.name: Update Chrome if the menu looks different
steps.text: Select More, then Help, then About Google Chrome. Chrome checks for an update on that page. If one is ready, select Relaunch to apply it.
steps.tip: Choose Not now to wait until your next restart.

shortcuts.action: Move the cursor to the address bar

troubleshooting.problem: No Translate icon in the address bar
troubleshooting.fix: Refresh the page using the reload button to the left of the address bar, then look again. Check Settings, Languages, and the never list for the page language. If the icon still does not show, use the right-click menu on the same page.

troubleshooting.problem: No Translate to option in the right-click menu
troubleshooting.fix: Make sure Use Google Translate is turned on under Settings, Languages, Google Translate. Refresh the page, then right-click an empty part of the page again.
Refresh the page and translate again. Google's help article names refresh as the first fix when translation doesn't work. If it keeps happening, update Chrome and try the same page in a new tab.
Machine translation sometimes picks the wrong meaning. Check the original for names, figures, and short phrases. Translate a single sentence with Translate selection to to compare.

troubleshooting.problem: The text is in a Mac app, not a web page
troubleshooting.fix: Chrome translates web pages in its tabs, not text in other apps. Copy the text into translate.google.com, or hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur what the text says.
